name: Omar Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Omar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and anything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Stonebridge by half six. We've got three hundred sows outdoors, in fields with little tin huts we call arks. I go round with the feed on the quad and trailer, check the water, look for any sow that's lame or off her food. Afternoons, in season, I help Piotr with the sprayer on the wheat and rapeseed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove lorries for twenty-four years, grain and fertiliser mostly, all over. At fifty-five I had a heart scare on a motorway lay-by, and the doctor said no more long hauls. I knew the Kowalski brothers from delivering to them, and they said come and work the pigs. I said I don't know pigs. They said you'll learn.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Slowly. I still can't tell a sow that's about to farrow just from how she's walking, which Tomasz can from a hundred metres. What I like is it's local. I'm home for tea with Lena every night, which I never was in twenty-four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, so much for the robots, and probably have a laugh about it with the brothers. Maybe I'd share some funny article on the family group chat. I'm not one for arguing about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I'm doing until I retire. I use the AI a bit, my son Adrian showed me how to ask it about feed rations, and that's handy. If that's as far as it goes, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Stonebridge. Maybe I'd ask about doing my spraying certificate properly, so I can run the sprayer on my own and not just help Piotr. We'd keep saving the bit we save, maybe a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet stretch of motorway at night. You can just drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI is handy for feed. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter some of the sows were losing condition, getting thin. I asked it what might cause that in cold weather, and it said check the energy in the ration and the bedding. Tomasz said the same thing, but it helped me understand why, without having to ask him for the tenth time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So nothing in this picture worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The usual things: pig prices, the bank, whether the brothers want to keep going. Nothing to do with computers.

S0.say: I'd say so much for the robots and have a laugh with the brothers, maybe share a funny article on the family group chat.
S0.think: He keeps doing what he's doing until he retires, using AI a little for feed questions as his son showed him.
S0.do: Keeps working at Stonebridge and asks to get his spraying certificate so he can run the sprayer alone. Keeps saving about 150 a month.
S0.feel: Calm, like a quiet stretch of motorway at night.
S0.quote: It helped me understand why, without having to ask him for the tenth time.
S0.fieldNote: Omar values AI mainly as a way to save face while he learns, not as a big change. His worries in a plateau are ordinary farm worries. The move from lorry to farm after a heart scare shapes a gentle, unhurried outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so we might as well get it right. I'd say that at the pub, to the lads who say it's all nonsense, and to the ones who think it's the end of the world. Somewhere in the middle, like usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the pigs would be fine for a while. The brothers are careful with money. They still use a sprayer from 2009. They'd wait till they'd seen a neighbour's robots work for a couple of years, same as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the neighbours bought, then ask the brothers to let me learn whatever they choose. I'd use the AI a bit more, the way Adrian showed me, for the paperwork and the pig records. And we'd put a bit more by, two hundred a month, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just keeping an eye on the mirror.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Piotr, the younger brother. He's forty-five and the sprayer's his pride and joy. If a robot sprayer comes, that's his favourite job gone, not mine. He'd take it harder than me, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and act faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Tomasz came to me and said they're looking at a feeding robot. Then I'd go straight to the farm that has one and learn how it breaks down, because the one who knows how to fix it doesn't get let go.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming either way so we might as well get it right, somewhere in the middle between the doubters and the doom-mongers.
S1.think: He thinks the pigs are safe for a while, because the brothers are careful with money and still use a 2009 sprayer.
S1.do: Waits to see what neighbours buy, then asks to learn whatever the brothers choose. Uses AI more for paperwork and pig records and raises savings to about 200 a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, keeping an eye on the mirror.
S1.quote: The one who knows how to fix it doesn't get let go.
S1.fieldNote: Omar's trust in his bosses' caution is his main source of calm. He thinks about Piotr's pride before his own job. He has a clear trigger for acting faster: the brothers mentioning a feeding robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and we need some kind of help for people in the middle of it, without anyone going crazy. I'd say it to the brothers, and to Lena's customers when I pick her up from the salon. Not on social media, I don't go in for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Sixty, no lorry to go back to because they'd be driving themselves, and pigs that a robot can feed. Lena's salon would still bring something in, people still want a person cutting their hair, I think, but it's not enough for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back: the caravan goes, no holiday, the second phone line goes. I'd do odd jobs on the side, fixing fences and gates for people, while there's still demand. And I'd ask Daria and Adrian if they'd help if it came to it, which they would, though I wouldn't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Very anxious. But I wouldn't be lying on the floor. I've had worse days, like the day in the lay-by with my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the brothers were slow to buy new things. Does that help in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe two. But if everyone else has robots and their pork is cheaper, the brothers have to follow or go under. Being slow saves you for a while, and then it costs you everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years of warning, what would you be doing in the first six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asking the brothers straight, are you buying or selling? And getting my house in order, literally. The roof needs doing, and I'd get that done while I still have a wage, before it all happens.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and people in the middle of it need help, without anyone going crazy. He'd say it to the brothers and Lena's customers, not online.
S2.think: He'd be scared: 60, no lorry driving to fall back on, pigs a robot could feed. Lena's salon would bring something in, but not enough for both.
S2.do: Sells the caravan and cuts holidays and the second phone line straight away, and takes odd jobs fixing fences and gates. Gets the roof done while he still has a wage and asks his grown children for help if needed.
S2.feel: Very anxious but not floored; he's had worse days, like the heart scare in the lay-by.
S2.quote: Being slow saves you for a while, and then it costs you everything at once.
S2.fieldNote: Omar's anxiety is cushioned by Lena's salon income and the memory of surviving a heart scare. He spots that his bosses' caution only buys time. Fixing the roof while he still has a wage is a very concrete, practical move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not panic, but let's not sit on our hands either. I'd say it at the pub and at the brothers' kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years feels more manageable. I'd be sixty-three, and if the brothers keep me on until the robots are bought, maybe I'd stop at sixty-four with a bit put by. It depends on whether they keep going at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving, two hundred a month, and once the first neighbours had the feeding robots working, I'd ask to go and learn them. I'd talk to the brothers about whether I could become the one who checks the robots and does the jobs they can't, like the farrowing. And I'd plan to take my pension at sixty-four, even if it's a bit less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More time means more chances to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me time to watch the neighbours. With two years, everything happens at once and nobody knows what works. With five, someone else makes the mistakes first, and I learn from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Adrian. He works in a warehouse office doing the logistics, and that's the sort of job these things eat. I'd tell him what I learned in the lorry: when the company starts talking about efficiency, update your licence.

S3.say: I'd say we've got five years, so no panic, but no sitting on our hands either. I'd say it at the pub and at the brothers' kitchen table.
S3.think: Five years feels more manageable; at 63 he might stop at 64 with something put by, if the brothers keep the farm going at all.
S3.do: Keeps saving about 200 a month and, once neighbours have feeding robots working, asks to learn them. Offers to be the person who checks the robots and handles farrowing, and plans to take his pension at 64.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with more time meaning more chances to get ready.
S3.quote: With five, someone else makes the mistakes first, and I learn from them.
S3.fieldNote: Omar's steady style fits the five-year picture well: he wants others to test the technology first. His advice to his son Adrian draws on his lorry years. Whether the brothers keep the farm at all remains his big unknown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort it out sensibly. I'd say that to anyone who asked, and I'd tell the brothers to plan for it, not wait for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, I'd be retired. Sixty-eight is past when I'd stop. I'd probably still go round on a Saturday to help with the pigs, because I'd miss them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Stonebridge and help the brothers try the new machines once they're proven, to make the handover easy. I'd keep saving and pay off the last of the mortgage. And I'd spend more time with the grandson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like a road closure announced a year early. You just take a different route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still bother you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm itself. If the brothers sell up because some big company can run pigs cheaper with robots, the land goes to strangers. Tomasz's father built those arks with his own hands. That would be a shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's six. I'd tell him to be good with his hands and with people. I drove a lorry for twenty-four years and never once thought it would drive itself. Now I'm told the pigs might feed themselves too. I've stopped betting against it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to sort it out sensibly, and I'd tell the brothers to plan for it, not wait for it.
S4.think: He'd be retired by 68, past when he planned to stop, so the robots wouldn't touch his working life. He'd maybe still help with the pigs on Saturdays because he'd miss them.
S4.do: Keeps working at Stonebridge and helps the brothers try proven machines to ease the handover. Keeps saving, pays off the last of the mortgage and spends more time with his grandson.
S4.feel: Calm, like a road closure announced a year early.
S4.quote: Tomasz's father built those arks with his own hands.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Omar's worry moves from himself to the farm and the family who run it. He sees himself helping with the handover rather than resisting it. His advice to his six-year-old grandson, hands and people, is short and grounded.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Sixty, no lorry, no pigs, three or four months of savings. What would help is some help for small family farms like Stonebridge to keep older workers on alongside the machines, and a pension that can start a few years early for people whose work gets taken over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about health. Half of why I'm here is my heart. A lot of men my age are on farms because the doctor said slow down. If the robots take these jobs, where do we go to slow down?

headlineQuote: I drove a lorry for twenty-four years and never once thought it would drive itself. Now I'm told the pigs might feed themselves too. I've stopped betting against it.
portrait: Omar Novak is 58, a former long-distance lorry driver who switched to farm work three years ago after a heart scare and now works with the outdoor pigs and the sprayer at Stonebridge, an arable and pig farm run by two brothers. He is still learning, uses AI tools now and then when his son shows him something useful, and takes up new kit once he's seen it work on someone else's farm. He is pragmatic and even-handed, blaming nobody and trusting his bosses' loyalty more than any policy. He stays calm through a plateau, uneasy with steady change, and anxious with AGI in two years, softened by his wife Lena's salon income and the brothers' slowness to spend. With five or ten years he plans to learn the new machines when they've proven themselves and ease into retirement.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because at 60 he'd have no fallback, lorry driving would be gone too, and a few months of savings wouldn't bridge the gap to his pension.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small family farms to keep older workers on alongside the machines, and a pension that can start a few years early for people whose work is taken over.
